title: S8 — Roads and Asphalt Paving

concepts.title: Pavement is a layered spring
concepts.mechanism: A road's job is to take a concentrated wheel load and spread it out, layer by layer, until it's gentle enough for the natural subgrade underneath to carry without deforming — the same load-path idea as a building, just sideways and spread out instead of straight down. Subgrade, base, and binder each spread the load a little wider before the surface course goes on top last, as a wear layer, not a structural one. Rush the surface course onto a base that isn't compacted and tested yet, and the load has nothing solid to spread onto — the whole layered spring collapses from the bottom.
concepts.mechanismPro: Each layer (subgrade → base → prime → binder → surface) distributes load over a widening area; surface course is always last and is a sacrificial wear layer, not the structural element — base compaction (often ~98%) and proof-rolling must be verified before binder/surface proceed.
concepts.hook: A trampoline works because several layers — frame, springs, mat — share the load before you ever land. Skip straight to the mat without the springs underneath and you just hit the ground.

applied.prompt: The paver wants to lay the asphalt surface course to hit a deadline, before the base course has been proof-rolled and density-tested.

options.label: Hold the surface course until base compaction/proof-rolling confirms it meets spec
options.outcome: Right. The surface is the sacrificial top layer of a structural system — putting it down on an unverified base is finishing a spring with no coils underneath.

options.label: Spot-check the most suspect base areas and proceed on the rest if they pass
options.outcome: A workable risk reduction if the spot checks are genuinely representative — but any failed spot should stop that section, not just get noted.

options.label: Let the paver proceed to hit the deadline
options.outcome: An uncompacted base settles under traffic, and the road dips and cracks from the bottom up within a season — the exact 'layered spring' failure the module warns about, now buried under fresh asphalt.

applied.debrief: This is V3-1's load-path law spread sideways: every load needs an unbroken, adequate road to the ground, whether that's a column to a footing or a tire load through five pavement layers to the subgrade. Skipping a layer's verification is breaking the road.

summary: Pavement is a layered spring — subgrade, base, prime, binder, then (last, always last) the surface course. Asphalt is temperature-critical: the compaction window closes as the mat cools. And on an island, the paver mobilization economics say: batch the paving. PLAIN: layers, heat, and timing. PRO: 98% base, binder through construction, surface course as the sacrificial wear layer.

sections.heading: The layered spring
sections.body: PLAIN: A road is layers, each protecting the one below and supported by the one beneath: your rock subgrade (excellent) → compacted crushed-limestone base → a sticky prime coat so the asphalt bonds → the coarse structural binder course → and finally the fine surface course. The surface course is the SACRIFICIAL WEAR LAYER — the shoes of the road — and you don't wear your good shoes to pour concrete, which is the materials-science version of Module 3's finishes-last rule. PRO: base 6–8 in at 98% Proctor; binder 1.5–2.5 in; surface 1–1.5 in placed after construction traffic ends; crown/cross-slope 2% to swales and drainage wells — ponding on a new road is a grade-survey failure, not bad luck.

sections.heading: Temperature is the whole game
sections.body: PLAIN: Asphalt arrives hot (~275–300°F) and can only be compacted while it stays hot enough to move (~above 175°F) — thin lifts on breezy days cool in MINUTES, so the rollers follow the paver immediately, not eventually. PRO: breakdown, intermediate, and finish rolling passes in sequence behind the paver; density verified by cores or gauge at 92–96% of theoretical max; joints — longitudinal and transverse — are the failure-initiation points, so hot joints and proper overlap matter. Cores at 1 per 500–1,000 tons.

sections.heading: Island paving logistics
sections.body: PLAIN: Asphalt binder is imported and plants are few — paving happens when the plant runs, and sending a paver to do one cul-de-sac costs almost as much as a whole street day. So paving gets BATCHED: accumulated into campaigns that fill plant runs and amortize mobilization. PRO: paver mobilization $15–40K; asphalt $110–160/ton placed; schedule paving windows around plant runs and weather (no placement on wet base); the 'mobilize for one cul-de-sac' job is the unit-rate horror story every island QS tells.

quiz.teach: The surface course is the finest, prettiest, least structural layer.
quiz.prompt: Why does the surface course go down LAST — after years of construction traffic ran on the binder?

choices.text: It's the sacrificial wear layer — placing it before heavy traffic ends spends the road's finished skin on dump trucks, then you buy it twice
choices.why: Correct. The binder course is built to carry construction; the surface course is built to be the road buyers drive on. Sequence is the whole economics.

choices.text: The surface course needs the binder to cure for years first
choices.why: Asphalt doesn't cure like concrete — the wait is about TRAFFIC, not chemistry.

choices.text: Surface asphalt is a different plant product that's scarce
choices.why: It's a finer mix from the same plants. Availability isn't the driver; wear preservation is.
No regulation — just the finishes-last rule with a materials-science reason. The sim punishes early finishing because reality invoices it.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: don't put the good carpet down while the movers are still walking through. PRO: 'binder carries construction; mill and repair the binder's wounds; surface course in one batched campaign at the end.' (S8, M3)

quiz.teach: Compaction must finish before the mat cools below workable temperature.
quiz.prompt: Why do the rollers follow the paver IMMEDIATELY, and what happens on a windy, cool evening with a thin lift?

choices.text: The mat is only compactable above ~175°F, and a thin lift in wind loses that in minutes — rollers that lag produce a low-density mat that ravels and fails young
choices.why: Correct. The compaction window is a cooling curve; thin lifts + wind + cool air steepen it brutally. The roller schedule IS the quality plan.
Efficiency is incidental — below the cessation temperature, no amount of rolling achieves density. The window closes physically.

choices.text: It keeps the paving train compact for traffic control
choices.why: Logistics nicety; the driver is mat temperature. You can re-route traffic — you can't re-heat the mat.

choices.text: Nothing — asphalt can be re-rolled next morning
choices.why: Cold asphalt under a roller just cracks. Density not achieved in the window is not achievable, only removable.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: asphalt is only squeezable while hot, and it cools like coffee — faster in wind, faster when thin. PRO: 'place ≥275°F, compact before ~175°F; breakdown roller ON the paver's heels; watch thin lifts on windy days.' Density 92–96% TMD by core. (S8)

quiz.teach: Core results are the pavement's acceptance test.
quiz.prompt: Cores on a street come back at 90% of theoretical max density against a 92–96% spec. Accept with penalty, or remove?

choices.text: It depends on where and how much — isolated low cores in low-traffic areas often take a priced penalty (reduced pay, extended warranty); systematic lows or main-road failures get removed, because under-compacted mats fail young under load
choices.why: Correct. Acceptance-with-penalty exists because removal isn't free either — but it's a tool for MARGINAL, LOCALIZED shortfalls, not a discount program for bad paving.

choices.text: Always accept with penalty — 2% is invisible
choices.why: Density-to-life curves are steep: a few points of air voids can halve pavement life. The penalty must price the LIFE lost, and on main roads it usually can't.
Removing a whole cul-de-sac mat over one marginal core wastes money the penalty mechanism exists to save. Rigidity is not rigor.
The window closed weeks ago (see the cooling curve) — cold re-rolling cracks the mat. The choice is genuinely penalty or removal.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: a slightly-squishy road in a quiet corner can be paid for as slightly-worse; a squishy main road gets rebuilt. PRO: 'evaluate extent, location, and traffic; pay-factor the marginal, remove the systematic.' Your QA lab's cores are what make either answer enforceable. (S8, M12)

mathProblems.title: Surface course campaign
mathProblems.context: The final lift across the community: tonnage × placed rate, in one batched campaign — the payoff of protecting the binder for years.

mathProblems.title: The cul-de-sac mobilization tax
mathProblems.context: Piecemeal paving pays the paver mobilization repeatedly. Count the extra visits piecemeal paving would take and price the tax.

decisionPoints.title: Rutted binder under the final lift
decisionPoints.scenario: The binder course carried construction traffic for 14 months and shows rutting at two intersections plus scattered patches where utility crossings were cut. The surface-course campaign is mobilizing in three weeks. The paving sub offers: (a) mill and repave the damaged binder areas first, (b) a leveling course over the ruts, or (c) 'the surface course will hide it.'

options.label: Mill and repave the rutted intersections and failed patches, THEN the surface course over sound binder everywhere
options.outcome: The intersections — where every wheel brakes and turns — get a sound structure under the wear layer. 'Hide it' would have telegraphed every rut through the new mat within two summers; milling first is why the final lift stays flat for its design life.

options.label: Leveling course over the ruts, surface over everything
options.outcome: Cheaper than milling and workable where deformation is minor — but a leveling course over STRUCTURALLY failed binder (those intersections) is smoothing over movement that will continue underneath. Fine for the scattered patches; wrong for the intersections.

options.label: Let the surface course hide it — it's an inch and a half of new asphalt
options.outcome: Ruts reflect through thin overlays like handwriting through tracing paper — the deformation mechanism is still live below. Year two: the new road shows the old ruts, and now the repair means milling through the surface you just paid for.

decisionPoints.debrief: The binder course's construction wounds get REPAIRED, not carpeted: distress reflects through overlays because its cause survives underneath. Inspect the binder like a subgrade before the final lift — it is one. (S8)
